name: 74HC74 Dual D Flip-Flop
summary: Two edge-triggered D flip-flops with preset and clear. One bit of memory, a divide-by-two, or a proper synchronizer for an async input.
notes: D is captured on the RISING edge of the clock and held until the next one. That is the difference between this and a transparent latch like the 74HC373.
Tie Q-bar back to D and the output toggles on every clock: a divide-by-two with one gate. Chain them for a ripple counter.
PRE and CLR are both ACTIVE LOW and both asynchronous, meaning they override the clock entirely. Tie them high through a resistor if unused. Leaving them floating is why a flip-flop appears stuck.
Asserting PRE and CLR together is an illegal state: both outputs go high and the next release is a race. Never drive them from the same logic without interlocking.
This is the right part for bringing an asynchronous signal into a clocked system. Two in series, clocked by your system clock, resolves metastability to a vanishing probability.
The datasheet gives a setup time of 20 ns at 4.5 V, or 25 ns over the full -40 to 85 °C range. Data must be stable that long before the clock edge or the output is undefined.

pins.name: 1CLK
pins.note: Captures D on the rising edge.

pins.name: /1Q
pins.note: Tie this back to 1D for a divide-by-two.

circuit.title: Divide by two

parts.why: Inverted output back to D. Every clock edge flips the state, so the output runs at half the clock.
Preset is active low and has no internal pull-up. Floating, the flip-flop sets itself at random.
Clear is active low as well. Both have to be held high for the flip-flop to clock at all.

circuit.note: Chain the second flip-flop onto the first for divide by four. The output is also a clean 50 percent duty cycle whatever the input looked like, which is the other reason to do this.
